newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW - Japan's August current account.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Japan's August current account.

text.p: The following is a selection of analysts' reactions to Japan's current account data for August, released on Wednesday, which showed a year-on-year decline of 28.9 percent to 460.60 billion yen.
Analysts had anticipated that the August surplus would be between 404 billion yen and 510 billion yen, compared with a 648 billion yen surplus a year earlier.
JESPER KOLL, HEAD OF RESEARCH, J.P. MORGAN, TOKYO:
"They (the figures) are exactly as expected. And there is no surprise here."

Referring to the question of whether the rate of decline in the surplus would continue to slow, he said: "Short-term, my view is that any increase in demand will be met first with domestic supply because of the yen's depreciation and therefore the rate of decline (of the surplus) will continue to narrow over the medium-term."
"Once the yen starts to appreciate or domestic sources...reach their limit, import growth will pick up again. (But) it could be quite a while."

"You've got further evidence that import growth is outpacing exports. You've got import growth almost three times as fast as Japanese export growth and that's what's reducing the overall balance. On the capital flow account, we do see some evidence of Japanese appetite for international securities. However, it's a gradual pickup in capital outflows...I think we are going to see Japanese exports gaining momentum in the next four to six months. I would expect by the beginning of 1997 that the Japanese trade and current account surplus is going to start to actually grow again very gradually.
